% introduction.tex -- Section 1: Introduction

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Vision token pruning is one of the most reliable efficiency techniques in Vision Transformer (ViT) inference.
DynamicViT~\cite{rao2021dynamicvit} removes 66\% of patch tokens with less than 0.5\% accuracy loss on ImageNet classification.
Token Merging (ToMe)~\cite{bolya2023tome} merges 40\% of tokens while retaining over 99\% of classification accuracy.
EViT~\cite{liang2022evit} discards 50\% of inattentive tokens with negligible degradation.
These consistent results across architectures and benchmarks have established a strong prior: vision tokens are highly redundant, and aggressive reduction is safe.
A natural question follows.
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models~\cite{zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,shukor2025smolvla} use the same ViT encoders as their visual front-ends, producing hundreds of patch tokens that dominate the input sequence to the language model backbone.
For real-time robotic control, where inference latency directly constrains action frequency, reducing these vision tokens would yield immediate speedups in the most expensive component of the forward pass.
Does ViT token reduction transfer to VLA closed-loop control?

This question has practical urgency.
Current VLA models such as RT-2~\cite{zitkovich2023rt2} and $\pi_0$~\cite{black2024pi0} use large vision encoders that produce 256 or more tokens per image.
When multiple camera views are used, the vision token count grows proportionally.
In a typical deployment scenario, a VLA must produce actions at 5--10 Hz to maintain smooth control, and the LLM backbone's self-attention over vision tokens is the dominant latency bottleneck because attention cost scales quadratically with sequence length.
SmolVLA~\cite{shukor2025smolvla}, a compact 451.5M-parameter VLA, produces 256 vision tokens from two cameras (128 per view), and these tokens constitute the majority of the LLM backbone's input sequence.
Reducing the vision token count from 256 to 128 would cut attention FLOPs by approximately 4$\times$ for the vision portion of the sequence, a significant gain for real-time control.
Several recent works have begun exploring token efficiency for Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and VLAs, motivated by these potential speedups.
FastV~\cite{chen2024fastv} identifies and prunes inattentive visual tokens in VLM inference, achieving 2$\times$ speedup with minimal quality loss on VLM benchmarks.
VLA-Cache~\cite{hsu2025vlacache} caches vision tokens across timesteps to reduce redundant computation in temporal sequences.
VLA-IAP~\cite{wang2026vlaiap} proposes importance-aware pruning for VLA inference acceleration.
These proposals are motivated by the same intuition that has driven ViT pruning: if many vision tokens contribute little to the output, removing them should provide efficiency gains at minimal performance cost.
The implicit assumption is that the redundancy structure observed in ViT classification (where attention concentrates on a few discriminative patches) also holds in VLA models.

Despite this growing interest, no prior work has systematically evaluated how inference-time vision token reduction behaves across different VLA architectures in closed-loop control.
Existing evaluations of VLM token reduction rely on offline metrics such as action loss, perplexity, or next-token prediction accuracy~\cite{chen2024fastv,wang2026vlaiap}.
These proxies measure average-case behavior over individual timesteps but do not capture the compounding effects of action errors in closed-loop execution, where a single bad action can move the robot into an unrecoverable state.
The distinction between open-loop and closed-loop evaluation is well-established in robotics: policies that achieve low imitation loss can still fail catastrophically when errors compound across timesteps in the absence of corrective demonstrations.
The robotics community currently lacks empirical guidance on whether vision token reduction is a viable efficiency strategy for deployed VLA policies, and whether the answer depends on architectural choices that vary across models.

We conduct the first systematic closed-loop evaluation of this question across two VLA architectures.
On SmolVLA (451.5M parameters, pixel-shuffle vision connector), we test six pruning configurations spanning three axes: scoring function (learned importance scorer vs.\ random), retention ratio ($k \in \{0.5, 0.7, 0.9\}$), and mechanism (zero-masking, true removal, token merging).
Every configuration collapses to 0\% Success Rate (SR) across 500 episodes (Wilson 95\% CI: [0\%, 0.76\%]), compared to a 44.8\% baseline.
Even retaining 90\% of tokens produces complete task failure.
We term this the \emph{cliff-edge}: a binary transition from functional to non-functional with no intermediate regime.
On OpenVLA (7B parameters, MLP projector), the same 50\% random token removal yields 37.4\% SR against a 74.0\% baseline, a proportional 49.5\% relative drop with graded, task-dependent degradation.
The divergence is striking: identical pruning operations cause catastrophic failure in one architecture and graceful degradation in another.

The key architectural difference lies in the vision connector.
SmolVLA's pixel-shuffle connector applies $4{\times}4$ spatial folding, compressing 1024 SigLIP patches into 64 tokens per camera by channel concatenation.
Each resulting token encodes 16 spatially contiguous patches, creating inter-token dependencies that make every token indispensable.
The attention entropy ratio confirms this: SmolVLA's action decoder attends to vision tokens near-uniformly (entropy ratio 0.98), while OpenVLA's deep layers concentrate attention on a small subset of its 256 independently projected tokens (entropy ratio 0.617, dropping to 0.37 in the deepest layers).
High entropy means uniform reliance on all tokens; low entropy means the model has learned to identify which tokens matter, and the rest can be safely removed.

This architectural diagnosis points to a solution.
If the cliff-edge arises because pixel-shuffle tokens carry irreplaceable information, then compression should aggregate rather than delete.
We train a cross-attention pooling module (Smart Compress) that maps SmolVLA's 128 vision tokens to $M$ learned query vectors, where each query attends over all source tokens.
At $M = 32$ (75\% token reduction), Smart Compress achieves 61.6\% SR (CI [57.3\%, 65.8\%]), exceeding the uncompressed baseline of 44.8\% by 16.8 percentage points.
At $M = 64$ (50\% reduction), performance is identical at 61.6\%.
In the same setting where every hard pruning method produces 0\%, learned compression not only avoids the cliff-edge but improves over no compression.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Architecture-dependent compressibility} (Section~\ref{sec:results}): We present the first cross-architecture closed-loop evaluation of VLA vision token reduction, revealing that compressibility is determined by the vision connector design. Pixel-shuffle connectors produce cliff-edge failure (44.8\% $\to$ 0\%); MLP projectors allow graded degradation (74.0\% $\to$ 37.4\%).
    \item \textbf{Mechanistic explanation} (Section~\ref{sec:analysis}): We trace the divergence to the connector's effect on token information density and attention distribution. We propose the attention entropy ratio as a lightweight, architecture-agnostic predictor of compressibility (0.98 = incompressible, 0.62 = compressible).
    \item \textbf{Learned compression overcomes the cliff-edge} (Section~\ref{sec:smart_compress_results}): For architectures where hard pruning fails, cross-attention pooling achieves 61.6\% SR at 75\% token reduction, converting a non-functional operating point into one that exceeds the uncompressed baseline.
    \item \textbf{Offline metric disconnect} (Section~\ref{sec:metric_disconnect}): We demonstrate that standard offline evaluation proxies provide misleadingly optimistic estimates, establishing that closed-loop evaluation is essential for validating VLA compression techniques.
\end{enumerate}

6	This section describes the architectures and benchmark used in our study: SmolVLA~\cite{shukor2025smolvla} and OpenVLA~\cite{kim2024openvla}, two VLA models with contrasting vision connector designs, and the LIBERO benchmark~\cite{liu2023libero} on which we evaluate closed-loop performance.

8	\subsection{SmolVLA Architecture}
9	\label{sec:smolvla_arch}
10	
11	Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models cast robotic control as conditional generation: given a camera observation and a language instruction, the model predicts a continuous action.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

\paragraph{Vision token efficiency.}
Token pruning in Vision Transformers is well established.
DynamicViT~\cite{rao2021dynamicvit} learns a binary mask to remove tokens progressively across layers, EViT~\cite{liang2022evit} fuses inattentive tokens guided by CLS attention, and ToMe~\cite{bolya2023tome} merges tokens via bipartite matching without any training.
These methods consistently remove 30\%--60\% of tokens with less than 1\% accuracy loss on ImageNet classification.
For Vision-Language Models, FastV~\cite{chen2024fastv} prunes visual tokens after early LLM layers based on attention patterns, and LLaVA-PruMerge~\cite{shang2024prumerge} combines CLS-attention pruning with similarity-based merging to reduce tokens by 4$\times$ on VQA benchmarks.
Our work tests whether these results transfer to closed-loop VLA control, where action errors compound across timesteps.

\paragraph{VLA-specific token reduction.}
Three concurrent works address token efficiency in VLA models.
VLA-Cache~\cite{hsu2025vlacache} caches vision token KV states across timesteps, exploiting temporal redundancy in sequential observations to achieve 1.7$\times$ speedup without removing tokens.
VLA-IAP~\cite{wang2026vlaiap} proposes interaction-aligned pruning with geometric scheduling, reporting 97.8\% SR on OpenVLA with 1.54$\times$ speedup.
EfficientVLA~\cite{yang2025efficientvla} combines layer pruning, task-aware token selection, and temporal caching for 1.93$\times$ speedup on CogACT.
VLA-Pruner~\cite{liu2025vlapruner} uses dual-level importance criteria combining semantic and action-level attention for temporal-aware pruning.
A critical distinction is that VLA-IAP and EfficientVLA evaluate on models with MLP projectors (OpenVLA, CogACT), which we show exhibit graded degradation under pruning.
None of these works evaluates token reduction on pixel-shuffle VLAs, and none reports the cliff-edge failure we observe on SmolVLA.
Our findings suggest that their positive results may not generalize to architectures with spatially entangled vision connectors.

\paragraph{Vision connectors in multimodal models.}
The design of the vision-to-language connector varies substantially across models and has direct implications for token compressibility.
Linear or MLP projectors~\cite{liu2023llava,kim2024openvla} map each vision encoder patch independently, preserving per-token granularity.
Cross-attention connectors such as Q-Former~\cite{li2023blip2} and the Perceiver Resampler~\cite{alayrac2022flamingo,jaegle2021perceiver} compress visual features into a fixed set of learned queries, reducing token count at the architectural level.
Pixel-shuffle connectors~\cite{shi2016subpixel}, adopted by SmolVLA~\cite{shukor2025smolvla} and InternVL~\cite{chen2024internvl}, apply spatial folding to compress patches via channel concatenation, achieving high compression during training but creating inter-token dependencies.
Our analysis reveals that this connector taxonomy also determines inference-time compressibility: MLP projectors tolerate post-hoc pruning, pixel-shuffle connectors do not, and cross-attention connectors provide a solution for the latter case.
To our knowledge, no prior work has connected vision connector design to token pruning robustness in the VLA setting.
